lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: I'd like to call this meeting to order. Welcome here, everyone. And at this time, I'd like to give the opening to Councillor Michael Zwaagstra.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Over the last weekend has been an exciting weekend in our city. That's because it's— the Southeast Event Centre held its first public event Last weekend, Friday night, the Pistons game, and then of course another game on Saturday. And everything that I'm hearing, whether I'm seeing posts online or talking to people in person, is that people are pleased with what they are seeing. This event centre definitely has the wow factor. And it's important to note, it's not even completely open yet. Only the arena portion is open. We still have other components that need to be finished off over the, the coming weeks. It's been a long process getting to this point. What I want to do today is I want to highlight 6 decisions that were made in the past that have played a key role in getting to where we are now. This is not a comprehensive history of the Events Centre. Rather, looking over the last number of years, I just want to highlight 6 things that stand out to me, uh, that, uh, that if any one of these 6 things had not happened, it's entirely possible that the Southeast Events Centre would not be open in its current location today. First decision: buying land downtown. Now, I'm not even exactly sure when this began, but the information that I have is that it likely was in the early 1990s when council started to purchase properties in the downtown area. Now, at the time when this decision was made, council back then had no idea what was going to go there. They just knew that it made sense for the city to strategically buy land in the downtown area for a future project of some sort. When I was first elected to council in 2006, and when the next property became available, it was simply explained to me that this is something council has been doing for a long time and that we don't know for sure what's going to go there, but that we should continue doing it. And I have to say, I give full credit to whichever council it was that first started that in the 1990s, because without that long-term commitment of council after council buying land And how many properties are we talking about? I'd say probably 20 or 30. It's a lot of properties over the years. Without that land, there is no way that the Southeast Event Centre would be there in the current location. Second major decision: our 5-year borrowing policy. This was set in place during the 1980s when Helmut Pankratz was mayor, and the context at the time was that Steinbach was in a lot of debt in the 1980s, as were many municipalities. And that's because interest rates were incredibly high. This was the era of, you know, 16%, 18% mortgages. And so in response to those high debt levels and the high interest rates that contributed to it, council put in place a policy saying that the city will do all borrowing on a 5-year basis so that any project that's built will be paid off in 5 years. That policy put the city in a solid fiscal foundation. Thank you. I, I think it's unlikely that we'd be able to do the project that we're doing now if we hadn't had that policy for the last 30-plus years. Will we be able to keep to this policy forever? I suspect there is some projects coming up, thinking along wastewater, which will make it difficult to actually do that. But as far as a general practice with our facilities, a 5-year borrowing policy makes sense, which, by the way, we did do with With that event centre. It will be paid off in 5 years. Third major decision: the 2006 mayoral campaign pledge for a multiplex. Back in 2006, in both their respective mayoral campaigns, Chris Goertzen and Dwight Reimer publicly pledged to build a multiplex. You want to go pull out some old carillons, check out the ads? Both Goertzen and Reimer specifically put ads in saying, We want to build a multiplex. We want to build an event centre. And as far as I can tell, that was the first time that that pledge had been made publicly by a serious mayoral candidate. And so when Chris Goertzen was elected in an overwhelming mandate in 2006, this is something the council started talking about seriously. It was one of the first things that we started talking about. Didn't mean we could do it right away, but I don't think that we would have moved as far as we did If that pledge hadn't been made so clearly in 2006. Fourth major decision: the deal that we made with the Steinbach Credit Union. One of the— another issue that came up very early in my first term, and Councillor Jac Siemens will remember this too, is that the Steinbach Credit Union was going to build a new headquarters. And there was some serious discussion about where is this going to go. Is it going to go downtown? Is it going to be somewhere else on the north end of Steinbach? Where is it going to go? could potentially not be in Steinbach. And I remember Mayor Goertzen saying to council in our initial closed meetings, we need to do everything we possibly can to convince the credit union to stay downtown. And those discussions with the credit union board led to a deal where we signed an agreement stating that we will facilitate the construction of a new curling rink, because they needed the old one for parking. And, uh, and of course, we eventually were able to build that curling rink attached to the T.G. Smith Arena. Thank you. The credit union also made a financial contribution to the city as well. I don't think we'd be doing what we're doing now if the credit union hadn't made that deal with us. 5th major decision, setting up the recreation reserve. I remember in 2012, council unanimously approved a 10% tax increase. And where did most of that money go? It went to a new recreation reserve. I believe it was about $800,000 a year at the time. And we would use that money, we would save it up, For a future event centre that we obviously— we didn't even have on the books yet. But Mayor Goertzen did an effective job of convincing council. Most of us, many of those councillors are here today, that we need to do that. And again, if we hadn't set the recreation reserve up, I don't think we'd be where we are today. Final major decision. This is one that involves everyone here on council. The deal that we made with the Southeast Events Group. In 2019, representatives from the city, met with SEG members to agree upon a framework for a downtown Southeast Event Centre. At that, at that initial meeting, Mayor Funk, myself, Councillor Hiebert were there where we had those initial discussions, and that laid the foundation for a future memorandum of understanding where we agreed that we would build an event centre if we got the necessary funding in place. 6 major decisions, some made by this group here, some made decades before us, all key decisions in getting to where we are today. As we anticipate the forthcoming grand opening of the Southeast Event Centre, let's not forget the many past decisions that made it possible to be where we are today. Thank you.

lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. The notice for rezoning bylaw 2261 affecting 189 Hanover Street in Steinbach. Both the owner of the property and the applicant of the rezoning application is [Resident 1]. Purpose of the application is to rezone the subject property from RLD residential low density to RMD residential medium density to permit a multifamily development to be constructed. Notices as are required under the Planning Act have been issued. There is 8 items of correspondence that are on file, 7 of which were in council's original agenda package and 1 additional item that was received today and also provided to councilors in their mail bins. There's also a report on file from community planning. Yes. Indicating no provincial concerns with the proposal. The subject property is currently vacant. However, it previously contained a single-family structure on the site, and the area along Hanover Street generally consists of single-family structures. However, the opposite side of the street from the subject is zoned C-1 commercial neighborhood zone. The proposed development would also be subject to the city's residential infill policy requirements. Recommendation from administration is that this bylaw be given second reading subject to any new evidence presented and also subject to the owner entering into a development agreement.

lines.title: Mayor

lines.text: Anything further? Any further of council? Anything in closing? Yeah, council, I would agree with Councillor Penner. This seems like a reasonable ask, straightforward. Council, today we have as delegation Michelle Vezitny, the director of economic development for the Steinbach Economic Development Corporation, and— Take the podium and— The mic is yours.

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: Perfect, thank you. Good evening and thanks for taking some time to hear from Steinbach Economic Development tonight. I'm here together with Christine Beaumont, who is the president of SED, and also Henry Nickel, who is the VP of SED. Do I have a device? Thank you. Perfect. Okay, so as the agenda states, we're going to look today at Steinbach Economic Development's impact. And we're going to, you know, take a look at 4 key areas. The first one being community leadership, the next education and training, the third investment attraction, and the fourth workforce development. Thank you. Community leadership. SED is driving impactful growth through visionary leadership and engaged participation in 90% of the core factors that define a healthy community, such as physician recruitment, safety, education, recreation, project and business development, and economic immigration, to name just a few. There is no other organization in the region that impacts decisions in nearly every aspect of community wellness.

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: I sit on the following committee—

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: Community— I sit on the following committees providing leadership, insight, and guidance from an economic development perspective. Firstly, Southeast Events Group. I'm a board member. This municipal asset, the Southeast Event Centre, brings people together via sports, entertainment, trade shows, conferences, et cetera. Thank you. SED promotes and markets the centre, resulting in a revenue stream that supports internal operations. For example, the Economic Developers Association of Manitoba conference will be hosted in Steinbach in June for the very first time. Secondly, I sit on the Steinbach Community Development Committee. Recently, Mayor Funk appointed me to the CDC. SED's expansive provincial, national, and international reach will unlock powerful investment attraction opportunities, driving future growth and economic expansion. Thirdly, Community Safety and Wellbeing Committee. I was a steering committee member. Safety and community wellbeing are critical qualities of life factors that set communities apart. A secure environment for employees and their families not only enhance workforce retention, But also drives business efficiency, fueling sustained growth and expansion. Meetings have now concluded, and I was honored to contribute. Southeast Region Transportation Initiative. Regular meetings have also concluded. Residents in the Southeast Region consider Steinbach as the second destination of choice, Winnipeg being the first. Rural municipalities continue to determine Transportation priorities with needs varying throughout the region. Revenue streams continue to be the key factor in determining transportation's next steps. And finally, I was appointed also by Mayor Earl Funk to be the chair of the mayor's physician recruitment and retention task force. Closing the family or primary care physician gap remains a pressing challenge. Currently, Steinbach requires 10 full-time equivalent primary care physicians, equating to approximately 30 bodies to meet the current need, and this statistic does not account for Steinbach's population growth or attrition. Moving to education and training, SETT is accelerating progress in establishing Steinbach as rural Manitoba's education and training hub. With confirmed projects set to deliver a net economic benefit of $2.9 million per training cycle. Steinbach Economic Development Corporation is at the forefront of education and training expansion, spearheading initiatives that directly enhance workforce readiness and economic growth. These initiatives not only create new career pathways for residents, but also attract talent, business, and investment to the region. By fostering partnerships with post-secondary educate— or post-secondary institutions, industry leaders, and government stakeholders, SED is ensuring that Steinbach remains a center for innovation, skills development, and long-term economic prosperity. Investment attraction. SED has propelled Steinbach's recognition as a premier destination for provincial, national, and international investment, achieving achieving a 200% increase in lead generation year after year since 2022. This surge in investment interest has led to increased business inquiries and strengthened investor confidence. For example, the SED website had over 630 more users in the month of February alone. As SED solidifies Steinbach's reputation as a thriving economic hub, we remain committed to driving investment attraction, fostering innovation, and ensuring long-term prosperity for the region. In 2024, CED identified the United Kingdom and Germany as target markets. With support from CanExport grant funding, CED is strategically focusing on key industries including agriculture and food processing, agtech, transportation, and building product and services. By targeting these high-growth sectors, CED aims to strengthen international business ties, attract foreign direct investment, and create new opportunities for local enterprise. This positions Steinbach as a globally competitive hub for innovation and economic development while enforcing the region's reputation as a leader in advanced manufacturing, agribusiness, and technology-driven industries. Looking ahead, SED remains committed to sustaining this momentum by continuing to attract highly qualified investments fostering entrepreneurship and driving long-term economic success. With a strong foundation and an ambitious vision for the future, Steinbach as the center of advanced agribusiness in Canada— Steinbach is well on its way to becoming a leading force in Manitoba's economic landscape. And finally, workforce development. SED drives workforce development with a direct economic impact exceeding $12 million annually, and this has been accomplished with the Rural Community Immigration Pilot Program. Steinbach is one of 14 communities selected by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada to participate in RCIP, which is the Rural Community Immigration Pilot, a key initiative aimed at tackling highly skilled top-tier workforce shortages fueling economic immigration in the region. It is quite a distinction to be selected as one of 4 new Canadian locations. CED is proud to manage RSIP without financial support from the federal government, relying entirely on international— relying entirely on internally generated funds. Steinbach's RSIP program is set to officially launch in April or May. Drawing insights from both employer feedback and regional labour market data, The program will prioritize 5 key industry sectors. Within these sectors, up to 25 National Occupation Classification, NOC, codes will be identified to ensure a focused and strategic approach. Businesses operating within these 5 priority sectors are encouraged to pursue employer designation under the program. Once designated, an employer can extend a formal offer of employment to a candidate Provided the candidate satisfies all eligibility criteria as determined by IRCC. This rigorous process ensures alignment with both regional economic immigration goals and federal immigration policies. Upon approval of the offer of employment, SED will issue the candidate a highly coveted letter of recommendation, or the proverbial golden ticket. Serving as the final requirement for the candidate to proceed with their application for permanent residency. It symbolizes a pathway to a brighter future, both for the employer and the candidate, as it seeks to attract highly skilled, top-tier talent that fosters economic viability for business. CED is a game changer for Steinbach, and CED is just getting started. As the project scales, so does the potential to strategically expand talent allocations driving an unparalleled economic impact for the region. I am in Ottawa in the beginning of April and will be meeting with IRCC's RCIP department in person. In closing, SED remains committed to fostering strong relationships while amplifying Steinbach's presence on both national and international stages. SED plays a pivotal role in driving economic development By leveraging strategic partnerships, targeted economic initiatives, and forward-thinking policies, SED ensures that Steinbach remains a premier destination for businesses, entrepreneurs, and investors seeking long-term success. At SED's core is the careful balance between ambitious growth and the preservation of Steinbach's unique identity. As the region continues to expand, SED remains dedicated to maintaining the city's strong community values, cultural heritage, and high quality of life. SED cultivates an environment where businesses can thrive. SED is not only shaping Steinbach's economic future, but it is also reinforcing its reputation as a leader in Manitoba's evolving business landscape. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Well, thank you, Michelle. Great presentation. I do have a question for you. I think I'd like to meet with you after you've been back from Ottawa 'cause I'd like a little more information and to understand ARCEP better. But my question to you is, when you talk about internally generated funds to fund this, where do the funds come from? Like, do— are the— is the employer required to fund part of this? Like, how do we, how do we, how do we get this once this, this is all picked? And, and obviously there's cost to bring the person from their country over. Where do those costs come out of?

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: So those costs, often for businesses, uh, you may have heard of LMIA, which is the Labor Market Impact Assessment. This is LMIA exempt. So when I speak about internally generated funds, that comes from the— from SEDS, I guess, revenue stream, which is the public sector support and the private sector support. So we're incorporating this project in with an internal process. So we don't receive any federal or provincial funding to manage this. A lot of the heavy lifting is on behalf of the employer. So the employer is responsible for the, I guess, the HR process and finding that candidate. So some of those, I guess those HR costs will already be a part of their business operations, but there is no cost for an employer to participate in this. Said is, like I said, kind of that, you know, we offer this golden ticket, which upon designation, We are that vessel to that permanent residency. And via this project, we are able to attract that highly skilled top-tier talent that may be missing from, you know, from enterprise in the region.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: So then basically, so we'll come out of the said—

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: Budget.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Revenue stream. You bet. Okay, so are you, is there a certain number of applicants you're looking at or? Like, are you like looking at 20, 10, 15, or is it open? What is the budget to bring everyone over?

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: So those allocations or seats are determined, predetermined by IRCC. So each community that is selected to participate, it is based on maybe population, it's based on a number of things within the country. So there is, I guess, a reallocation phase which will occur in fall. So if communities that have been selected, for example, have not been able to use their seats or the allocations, other communities who are seeking for more have the opportunity to bid, if you will, on those seats. So we have been tasked with a certain number of allocations and that will grow as this project expands.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor

lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Just following up on the, on the RCIP thing. So internally generated funds, that's, you know, from the SED budget. Is this a contributing factor in the reason that you're requesting in the upcoming year for the city to double the public contribution to SED? Is this one of the big factors behind that?

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation) [medium]

lines.speaker: Earl Funk

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor

lines.text: Following up on that, why wouldn't the businesses be required to pay For the employer, the benefit they're getting out of it. Why would taxpayers, for example, or why would SED be responsible for paying that versus the business that benefits from getting the employee?

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: That criteria is set by IRCC. So that was set out early on in the expression of interest and in the memorandum of understanding. There is in that agreement that the businesses They're not, I guess, expected to pay for this service. This is a tool in their toolkit so that they can grow, they can expand operations within the region via that highly skilled talent. So that criteria is determined by IRCC. So selected communities did not have the opportunity to, let's say, charge a fee for engagement.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. So obviously the budget for next year is not set yet. Council has not made a decision. Does this mean, like, if the budget, for example, let's say it remains the same in terms of the public contribution, does this mean that the Did you make changes in terms of the RCIP, or do you make changes in other areas? It's just a little surprising to have such a major change in approach and an extra thing that, you know, we sort of found out about after the fact, and it's going to impact your budget and then the ask to us. So I'm just wondering if you can expand on that a little bit.

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: IRCC indicated— so the expression of interest, so with the federal government, things take time. So the expression of interest was sent in July. So when you received that extended budget, I believe it was November-ish or so, we were only told, or we were all, yeah, we were only told by RCC that we were a selected community end of December, beginning of January. So because we are looking to expand, and this is a really key piece of an economic driver. If we are going to be awarded additional allocations, we are going to be looking for capacity. So currently we have hired a part-time person to manage the ins and outs of the day-to-day of it. I'm responsible for the memorandum of understanding, setting the program, et cetera, et cetera. But as far as facilitation goes, We will be looking in some way to not only expand the ask for the public sector, but also for the private sector. And that initiative is ongoing.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Just one more question. How many seats were you designated for this?

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: Because it's fluid and because it is something that is fluid, we attribute these seats to Back to circling to the $12 million investment. So how, so the seats, you can look at it from IRC's perspective. So we've been allocated a number of seats. We've also known through IRCC's data that it's not only the primary applicant, but it's their family that they're also bringing along. So that tertiary employment is also considered in this. So for every seat, you can multiply it by 3. Okay.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: So how many seats are you designated?

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: It's just a challenge that there's really an ask for taxpayer money to fund this federal program that's being downloaded onto the municipal level, and then we can't have any information.

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: Let me get back to you. I can ask IRCC if that's information. So for example, I did ask them last week if I was able to divulge, let's say, how many applications were in the province, and they say that is not public information. So let me get back to you.

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor

lines.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mayor. I find it very concerning that there's Veils of transparency that are being hidden with regards to that program. But I think we've talked about enough. lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: Right. So that is also a public announcement that is going to come out in the next couple of weeks. So as soon as that public announcement is launched, then we will— I'll be able to comment a little bit more on that.

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor

lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I have a question regarding interest from businesses, local businesses. How much interest is there? Are there a lot of people asking? I know this award was made a while back. Are you getting a lot of response from the business community?

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: For RCIP?

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor) [medium]

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: I'll just add a little bit to that. I'm also quite surprised that with this type of program that there wouldn't be federal funding and that it wouldn't be requested or required of us as a community to fund.

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: So when it comes to this program, it's very different. So you can divide it between immigration and settlement. So this is not a settlement program. This is an economic immigration program of which It is a pathway to permanent residency. I don't wanna say it's an expedited pathway to permanent residency, but it really looks at that. It really looks at that workforce. Now, I don't have the answer of why IRCC is not providing funding for it. They're providing support for businesses. They're providing support in that way. But it is just one component of the project that they just don't provide any funding for it.

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: The— I can't, not at this time. lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. So just to clarify, um, in regards to RCIP, I mean, when the announcement was made, I had not known about it prior to that announcement. lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: For the expression of interest part, no. There was communication throughout. We felt as an independent corporation that this fit within our mandate of what Steinbach Economic Development Does. So when we're looking at kind of that sweet spot of Steinbach Economic Development, we live, and we've talked about it before, we live to support workforce development, quality of life, business retention expansion, and investment attraction. So that holistic approach. So we made the executive decision at the board level to continue to apply for this project because we did feel that it met the mandate of what we were asked to achieve. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, I will, I will just— when we hear of federal programs and, and provincial programs, and then you— they say apply, but then we find out there's no funding. Even when there is funding, sometimes we cautiously go forward as City Council because often what happens is is those programs then become, they were, which were once part of the federal government or part of the provincial government and they were doing them, they now become downloaded to the municipal government. So we've seen that many, many times. We've been around this table for quite a while. We've seen that many times. I don't know if that's what's going to happen here because this is, is this a pilot project?

lines.speaker: Michelle Bezditny
lines.title: Director of Economic Development
lines.label: Michelle Bezditny (Director of Economic Development, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation)
lines.text: It is.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, so usually that's how they call it, pilot project, and then all of a sudden, the— it's great for the community, you get involved, and before you know it, you're funding it 100%. So I would like to know more about this and understand it better, and that's why when you get back from Ottawa, if we could sit down and talk, but it does scare me It does scare me when they send things out, roll it out, and there's no— sorry, there's no funding for it because that generally tells me they're planning to keep this long-term, but it's always going to be cost to the municipality. Okay. And maybe there's a spinoff too, but I need to understand more before I can make a good decision on it, and that's why I want to make sure you that we connect after you're back from Ottawa and you've actually been talking with them across the table so that we understand what's going on here. But yeah, you've got to, there is some concerns because this has happened to us before. We have, we've gone down this road, it all sounded good and well, voilà, now it's your responsibility, right? And we don't want that. That could, generally they're starting to roll things out and they have been for a while with, Affordable housing. And if that becomes— that's usually the province's— it's usually in their basket, but they're more and more, they're looking to the municipalities to take care of that, right? And so we have— we do have to be careful with those kinds of things. So, but I, again, I want to know more information so that we can make an educated decision on that. Thank you. lines.speaker: Christine Beaumont

Having spoken to employers in other regions where they were able to fit fill vacant positions by using this program, allowing even existing newcomers that are in the community and are in jobs already to be able to stay in those jobs. lines.speaker: Christine Beaumont
lines.title: SED Board President
lines.label: Christine Beaumont (SED Board President, Steinbach Economic Development Corporation) [medium]

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: I can offer a few if council would wish to hear them. The annual traffic count program is, as you said, Mr. Mayor, an annual event, and it seems to be more special than I understood it to be. However, the city has engaged the services of WSP Canada in my memory for the entirety of its process, and I believe that's now stretched over 27 years. And it has been able to provide the city with some valuable information and certainly information on trends to help it plan its infrastructure. Upgrades and investments going forward. I'll rather not talk to specifics, but we'll direct council towards the end of the summary. It starts on page 98 of council's agenda package, just identifying some trends as noted in section 4.1. The 2024 traffic counts were conducted over 4 days at the end of September and early October. Generally, the observations found on the PTH 12 North and Brandt Street corridor were that the overall 1-year and 2-year growth rates for the corridor were identical at actually -2.3%. There was quite a bit of variability in the 1-year growth rate, with rates varying from -16% to +11%. On the city's corridor along PTH Thank you. And then finally, between PTH 52 West and Main Street, the overall traffic volumes on that section generally increased by 2.2% over the 2023 counts. Moving on into section 4.3, the analysis did come up with several recommendations, and they are not listed in any particular priority or order, Yes. Okay. The study primarily focused around the city's signalized intersections. For example, PTH 12 North at Clearspring Centre/Golfair Road. It does operate generally acceptably. However, it was noted during the study that there's a certain timing sequence of the signals along PTH 12 that were identified as being Conflicting. And those recommendations have been forwarded to MTI for review. And our understanding is that Manitoba Transportation and Infrastructure is currently in process of reviewing those. A couple of other particular intersections of note, PTH 12 North at Superstore access and the co-op access. And there's some suggested treatments and improvements Yes. So we're looking at some improvements to that intersection that could result in improved traffic flows. It's also suggested that traffic volumes and operations at the intersection of PTH 52 West and Industrial Road be also monitored to see if there's any benefits that can be gained from revisions to that intersection. And then finally, on the next page, on page 100, The final recommendation is that traffic signal timing should be reviewed with MTI prior to the 2025 traffic counting study to confirm they are using what they term as fixed versus floating coordination mode. I'm not sure exactly what that means. However, I do understand enough of it for it to be related to the coordination of the traffic signals along the entire section of PTH 12. Thank you. PTH 12 with the hopes that it would improve traffic flows and make traffic flows more efficient. If council has any other questions, I'll try to answer them for you.
